Paper 1:
arXiv ID: 2610.21584v1
Title: Geometric Queries on Tessellation-Free Displaced Surfaces
Authors: Bing Xu, Yang Zhou, Brian Budge
Categories: cs.GR
Published: 2026-10-15 09:30:51+00:00
Updated: 2026-10-15 09:30:51+00:00
DOI: None
URL: http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21584v1
PDF URL: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21584v1
Abstract: Displacement maps encode fine geometric detail in compact textures and simplify surface authoring, but using them typically requires pre-tessellating surfaces into dense triangle meshes, incurring a heavy memory cost. Recent tessellation-free methods enable direct ray tracing. However, broader geometric queries such as surface sampling, specular manifold search, and closest-point queries remain less explored. Supporting these operations requires surface enclosures, area estimates, and normal bounds, which scalar height intervals alone do not fully provide. We present a first-order texture-space hierarchy that unlocks these queries directly without pre-tessellation. Each node stores a local affine height plane and a conservative residual bound, retaining spatial height variation that scalar minimum--maximum bounds discard. The plane and residual provide surface enclosures for intersection and distance searches, while the plane's height and slopes supply area estimates for sampling. Additional slope bounds support specular light-path search. Building on this representation, we develop query-specific traversal, pruning, and sampling algorithms, and demonstrate them in caustics rendering, sampling displaced emitters, and surface partial differential equation (PDE) solvers. We demonstrate memory savings over pre-tessellation and performance improvements over query-specific baselines, while retaining efficient ray tracing.

arXiv ID: 2610.21548v1
Title: Finite-Time Guarantees for Constrained Reinforcement Learning under Partial Observability
Authors: Valentina Zaccaria, Philip Jordan, Tingting Ni, Gian Antonio Susto, Maryam Kamgarpour
Categories: cs.LG
Published: 2026-10-15 09:12:27+00:00
Updated: 2026-10-15 09:12:27+00:00
DOI: None
URL: http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21548v1
PDF URL: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21548v1
Abstract: We study reinforcement learning in constrained partially observable Markov decision processes (CPOMDPs), where an agent maximizes reward subject to a cost constraint using only incomplete information about the underlying state. The lack of state observability may require optimal policies to depend on arbitrarily long observation-action histories, making planning and learning challenging. We leverage recent advances in finite-memory approximations of POMDPs and represent finite history windows as states of a constrained MDP. We then develop a primal--dual algorithm that provides the first non-asymptotic guarantees that jointly bound average reward suboptimality and constraint violation in the original CPOMDP. A key challenge is that this finite-window approximation affects both reward values and the set of feasible policies. Under a filter-stability assumption, we derive bounds relating optimality and feasibility in the finite-state model to those in the original CPOMDP, with approximation errors that decay geometrically with the window length. Experiments in partially observable gridworlds demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

Title: Quantitative validation of SMBI deposition profiles on EAST using experimentally constrained simulations
Authors: Yangdi Yu, Tianyang Xia, Jie Zhang, Jia Huang, Huimin Qi, Dazheng Li, Yanlong Li, Xiaoxue He, Xiaowei Mao, Hang Yu, Shuang Zheng, Haoyu Nan, Junyi Yang, Kaining Lin, the EAST team
Categories: physics.plasm-ph
Published: 2026-10-15 09:11:32+00:00
Updated: 2026-10-15 09:11:32+00:00
DOI: None
URL: http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21546v1
PDF URL: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21546v1
Abstract: Quantitative comparison between SMBI fueling simulations and experiments has long been hampered by the poor constraint on the effective source. Here, the particle increment per pulse is extracted experimentally and used to calibrate the simulation source. For EAST shot 71438, the density evolution from microwave reflectometry is analyzed for nine SMBI pulse groups. The SMBI-induced density increase is isolated from the background by comparing the rising and falling phases around each pulse group. Its radial profile peaks in the mid-pedestal region for every pulse group. Volume integration of this increment provides the experimental reference. The simulations use a multi-fluid model in the BOUT++ framework in which two transport operators are recast into conservative flux form, with the particle balance residual reduced to about 2% of the injected amount, and the perpendicular transport coefficients are constructed from the discrete radial flux balance, with the unphysical changes of the initial density and temperature profiles in source-free evolution reduced by an order of magnitude. For three cases sharing the same nominal molecular flux, the simulated deposition peak agrees with the experimental one in the relative pedestal coordinate. The simulated conversion of the injected particles at the end of the injection is slightly lower than the value inferred from the experiment, while the fraction retained at the end of the pulse is higher. The perturbation thus decays more slowly in the simulation, which we attribute to fast loss channels not represented in the model, such as parallel losses to the scrape-off layer. The edge electron temperature stays on the high-temperature plateau of the dissociation and ionization rate coefficients throughout the pulse, and the inward shift of the deposition with edge cooling reported earlier does not occur under the present conditions.

Abstract: GRB 251222A is a long-duration gamma-ray burst at a spectroscopic redshift of $z=3.171$. It was detected by the EP as the soft X-ray transient EP251222b before and during the gamma-ray emission. We consider a multiple-shell scenario in which a faster, narrower shell catches up with a slower, wider shell. We assume that the selected pulse groups trace different ejecta and that the late X-ray flare marks their collision. Under these assumptions, we represent the post-collision outflow by an effective merged core and an outer annular component. A joint fit to the multi-band afterglow gives a Lorentz factor of $Γ_c\approx293$ for the merged core and $Γ_{1,w}\approx228$ for the outer component. Abstract: One of the most striking aspects of a flat band is not merely its lack of dispersion, but that it reduces the single-particle kinetic energy to a very small scale, allowing interaction effects to become the dominant energy scale in the low-energy physics. This picture has underpinned concepts such as flat-band ferromagnetism, flat-band superconductivity, and localized magnons. A more fundamental question, however, remains. Flat bands belong to the language of single-particle or linear-spin-wave physics; whether they survive as protected sharp excitations in a genuine many-body quantum magnet, or merely provide a skeleton of spectral weight left by the noninteracting picture, remains unclear. We study the spin-1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the edge-centered honeycomb lattice to examine this question. In contrast to flat bands in geometrically frustrated magnets such as kagome, this lattice has a 2:3 sublattice imbalance that renders the intersublattice coupling matrix rectangular, whose null space gives rise to a flat band at the single-particle level. The same imbalance stabilizes a ferrimagnetic ground state through the Lieb--Mattis theorem and leads to an edge-site-localized flat magnon in linear spin-wave theory. Combining linear spin-wave theory, sign-problem-free stochastic series expansion quantum Monte Carlo, and stochastic analytic continuation, we find that quantum fluctuations transform this harmonic flat mode into a broad continuum whose centroid is about 1.55J and nearly dispersionless along the high-symmetry path. Sublattice imbalance thus offers an unfrustrated route that unifies flat bands and ferrimagnetism, and suggests that flat-band geometry organizes many-body spectral weight rather than giving rise to a protected quasiparticle.

Abstract: Multimodal reasoning systems increasingly assume that longer chain-of-thought (CoT) uniformly improves downstream grounding. We show that this assumption fails in referring audio-visual segmentation (Ref-AVS): simple queries can be harmed by excessive reasoning, creating an "overthinking trap" associated with phrase and localization drift, while genuinely ambiguous queries still benefit from multi-step reasoning. To systematically study this, we construct counterfactual reasoning-budget labels under a five-fold out-of-fold evaluation protocol. Our results recast adaptive Ref-AVS reasoning as a pre-decisional representation problem: before the first generated token, the generation-onset state contains linearly decodable information predictive of whether additional reasoning will improve segmentation. A linear probe predicts binary reasoning need with 70.1% accuracy, substantially outperforming text-only features and uncertainty-based proxy signals. As a router, the onset-state controller improves over downstream confidence routing and closely matches Short-then-Decide while using far fewer tokens. Proxy comparisons show that the onset representation contains predictive information not fully recovered by the evaluated hand-crafted features. Reusing this onset state for lightweight, single forward-pass routing reduces autoregressive token consumption by 60% while retaining about 96% of always-long performance. It further provides a cost-quality trade-off on $R^2$-AVSBench without target-label tuning, rather than an accuracy improvement over always-long. Error analysis links harmful long reasoning to phrase and localization drift, illustrating the benefit of bypassing unnecessary reasoning on simple queries. Ultimately, our results support efficient adaptive reasoning in Ref-AVS through pre-decisional internal representations.

Abstract: One of the most striking aspects of a flat band is not merely its lack of dispersion, but that it reduces the single-particle kinetic energy to a very small scale, allowing interaction effects to become the dominant energy scale in the low-energy physics. This picture has underpinned concepts such as flat-band ferromagnetism, flat-band superconductivity, and localized magnons. A more fundamental question, however, remains. Flat bands belong to the language of single-particle or linear-spin-wave physics; whether they survive as protected sharp excitations in a genuine many-body quantum magnet, or merely provide a skeleton of spectral weight left by the noninteracting picture, remains unclear. We study the spin-1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the edge-centered honeycomb lattice to examine this question. In contrast to flat bands in geometrically frustrated magnets such as kagome, this lattice has a 2:3 sublattice imbalance that renders the intersublattice coupling matrix rectangular, whose null space gives rise to a flat band at the single-particle level. The same imbalance stabilizes a ferrimagnetic ground state through the Lieb--Mattis theorem and leads to an edge-site-localized flat magnon in linear spin-wave theory. Combining linear spin-wave theory, sign-problem-free stochastic series expansion quantum Monte Carlo, and stochastic analytic continuation, we find that quantum fluctuations transform this harmonic flat mode into a broad continuum whose centroid is about 1.55J and nearly dispersionless along the high-symmetry path. Abstract: While graphene/n-type silicon (Gr/n-Si) and PEDOT:PSS/n-Si solar cells offer a cost-effective alternative to conventional photovoltaics, achieving simultaneous high power conversion efficiency (PCE) and long-term environmental stability remains a formidable challenge. Abstract: A confident detection of orbital eccentricity in gravitational-wave signals from black hole-neutron star systems would be a strong indicator of their dynamical formation origin. Abstract: Fractional spin excitations in low-dimensional and frustrated magnets are commonly associated with sporadic spin fluctuations, as observed in quantum spin liquids, spin ices, and other complex magnetic states. In this study, we investigate the spin dynamics in the amplitude-modulated magnetic ground state of AgCuVO$_4$, a spin-1/2 chain compound with competing intrachain interactions, by muon spectroscopy. Our data reveal a Gaussian decay of muon polarization that remains remarkably resilient against applied magnetic fields---a behavior often interpreted as evidence of emergent sporadic spin dynamics. However, density functional theory calculations of muon stopping sites and their quadrupolar level-crossing resonance spectra suggest an alternative mechanism: a two-state model where the muon randomly hops between two nearby sites, eventually equilibrating across both on a microsecond timescale via quantum delocalization. These findings provide a microscopic explanation for the field-resilient muon polarization and indicate that such behavior may not always stem from intrinsic spin fluctuations, but can also arise from non-equilibrium muon dynamics.

Abstract: Language-conditioned humanoid motion generation enables users to create and refine robot movements through natural language. The central challenge is to connect an underspecified request to concrete motion structure that can subsequently be revised relative to an accepted reference. Abstract: We investigate the potential of surface detector arrays to identify ultra-high-energy neutrinos using vertical air showers with zenith angle $θ\leq 60^\circ$, a region largely unexplored in current searches. The method exploits the enhanced electromagnetic component at ground level arising from energetic leptons produced in neutrino interactions. Using detailed air-shower and detector simulations, we show that observables sensitive to the electromagnetic and muonic content provide genuine discrimination between neutrino-induced and hadron-induced showers. This is demonstrated both with idealized shower quantities and with realistic detector-level signals based on water-Cherenkov and scintillator detectors. The corresponding neutrino identification efficiency is used to derive the effective mass and, primarily, the effective area of the array under background-rejection requirements appropriate to targeted multi-messenger searches. Although not competitive with inclined-shower searches under the stringent background rejection factors required for diffuse-flux analyses, this approach establishes the feasibility of a vertical detection channel, extending the field of view of surface arrays and providing a complementary tool for multi-messenger observations of transient sources.

Abstract: Embodied AI agents in Augmented Reality (AR) could enable more natural collaboration in immersive analytics by engaging users through spatial, conversational, and visual interaction. However, designing such agents requires careful attention to context. We propose a preliminary conceptual framework for context-aware design of embodied agents structured around three dimensions of spatial, social, and semantic. This framework is further categorised into embeddedness (how agents are situated in the contexts) and awareness (how agents perceive and respond to the contexts). arXiv ID: 2410.07343
Title: BBN Constraint on Heavy Neutrino Production and Decay
Authors: Yu-Ming Chen, Yue Zhang
Year: 2024
Abstract: We explore the big-bang nucleosynthesis (BBN) constraint on heavy neutrino that is a mixture of gauge singlet fermion and active neutrinos in the Standard Model. We work in the minimal model with only two parameters, the heavy neutrino mass $m_4$ and the mixing parameter $|U_{a4}|^2$, where $a=e$, $μ$, or $τ$ stands for the active neutrino flavor. We show that both the early universe production mechanism and decay products of the heavy neutrino are determined by $m_4$ and $|U_{a4}|^2$, with little room for further assumptions. This predictivity allows us to present a portrait of the entire BBN excluded parameter space. Our analysis includes various effects including temporary matter domination, energy injections in the form of charged mesons, photons and light neutrinos. The BBN constraint is complementary to terrestrial search for heavy neutrinos (heavy neutral leptons) behind the origin of neutrino masses and portal to the dark sector.

brief.summary: The focused arXiv search found one directly relevant 2024 analysis, Chen and Zhang’s study of BBN limits on heavy neutrino production and decay (arXiv:2410.07343), but no clearly relevant 2025–2026 keV-sterile-DM-plus-BBN paper was returned. That work treats mass and active–sterile mixing as the only parameters and includes temporary matter domination, meson/photon/neutrino injection, and flavor dependence; its BBN-excluded region is complementary to laboratory HNL searches (https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.07343). For keV sterile-neutrino dark matter, BBN is generally not the dominant constraint when the particle is sufficiently long-lived: X-ray decay limits, phase-space and Lyman-alpha structure limits, and the relic-abundance mechanism usually control viability. The simplest non-resonant Dodelson–Widrow production scenario is widely regarded as excluded or highly disfavored by the combination of X-ray and small-scale-structure constraints, while viable possibilities remain in resonant production with a lepton asymmetry, mixed cold-plus-warm models, or models with additional interactions; the precise surviving bands depend strongly on the production assumptions and adopted structure-formation data.

The arXiv abstract search returned substantial older literature and only one directly relevant paper from 2024–2026; several broad searches were contaminated by irrelevant records and apparent future-dated entries, so claims about 2025–2026 coverage should be treated cautiously.

The available tools provide metadata and abstracts rather than full papers or numerical exclusion tables. They are sufficient to identify papers and reproduce the conceptual analyses, but not to quote exact exclusion contours from the papers.

No exact numerical viable mass–mixing boundary can be justified from the returned abstracts alone. A defensible conclusion is qualitative: minimal non-resonant keV production is strongly constrained, whereas resonant or nonstandard-production regions can survive; BBN-specific restrictions become central for heavier, unstable MeV–GeV sterile neutrinos.

For a final quantitative viability plot, the analysis should specify the production mechanism, dark-matter fraction, flavor structure, nuclear-rate dataset, observational deuterium and helium likelihoods, X-ray dataset, and Lyman-alpha prescription.

directions.goal: Survey 2024–2026 arXiv literature directly addressing sterile-neutrino dark matter, BBN constraints, and the surviving mass–mixing parameter regions.
directions.rationale: The key scientific distinction is between keV sterile-neutrino dark matter, for which BBN is often subdominant to X-ray and structure-formation limits, and heavier MeV–GeV HNLs, for which late decays and energy injection can strongly constrain BBN. This direction should establish what has actually been published recently and extract quantitative viable regions rather than extrapolating from older reviews.
steps: Search arXiv using focused combinations of sterile neutrino dark matter, BBN, keV, heavy neutral lepton, resonant production, X-ray, Lyman-alpha, and 2024–2026 date filters.
Use arxiv_agent to identify directly relevant 2024–2026 papers and distinguish new analyses from review, phenomenology, or unrelated oscillation papers.
Prioritize and download full text for arXiv:2410.07343 and any newer papers on keV sterile dark matter plus BBN, resonant or mixed production, modified interactions, and HNL decay constraints.

Read the full text of the highest-priority papers in chunks, extracting explicit mass ranges, mixing limits, abundance assumptions, flavor dependence, decay lifetimes, decay temperatures, and BBN observables.
Use the literature to separate constraints on |U_es|^2, |U_mus|^2, and |U_taus|^2 from one-angle sin^2(2theta) presentations, recording the convention used in each paper.
Extract figures and captions only for the principal exclusion or allowed-region plots, especially mass–mixing planes and plots combining BBN with laboratory, X-ray, or structure constraints.

Check whether each claimed viable region corresponds to all of the dark matter or only a subdominant fraction, and record the production mechanism: Dodelson–Widrow, Shi–Fuller, mixed cold-plus-warm, freeze-in, freeze-out, or nonstandard interactions.
Compare papers published in 2024, 2025, and 2026 separately; if no directly relevant 2025–2026 paper is found, document the search coverage and avoid presenting older results as recent.

Cite papers with validated verbatim evidence and synthesize a final table containing mass scale, mixing range, production assumptions, BBN status, X-ray status, structure-formation status, and whether the region remains viable.

Perform a robustness check across alternative assumptions about lepton asymmetry, warm fraction, structure-formation limits, and flavor mixing, emphasizing which conclusions are model-independent and which are not.
success_criteria: A cited inventory of relevant 2024–2026 arXiv papers, with explicit identification of the papers that genuinely analyze both sterile-neutrino dark matter and BBN.
A quantitative summary of surviving regions in mass–mixing space, separately for keV dark matter and heavier late-decaying HNLs.
Clear separation of all-DM versus subdominant-DM scenarios and of minimal versus nonstandard production.
Explicit treatment of electron, muon, and tau mixing where the literature provides it, including the relevant mixing convention.

A defensible conclusion about whether BBN, X-ray decay, phase-space, Lyman-alpha, or relic-abundance requirements dominate in each mass regime, supported by citations and extracted plot captions where useful.

directions.goal: Build a cross-checked phenomenological map of viable sterile-neutrino parameter space by comparing recent BBN analyses with the established X-ray, relic-density, and structure-formation constraints.
directions.rationale: A literature survey can overstate viability if it reports a BBN-allowed region without imposing dark-matter abundance, radiative-decay, and small-scale-structure constraints. This direction should test the recent claims against the main production scenarios and identify which surviving bands are conditional rather than robust.
steps: Search arXiv for recent papers on resonantly produced mixed sterile-neutrino dark matter, non-resonant production, neutrino self-interactions, freeze-in or freeze-out, and HNL BBN decay constraints.

Read the most relevant recent papers together with benchmark references such as arXiv:2306.16532, arXiv:2112.00758, arXiv:2204.08795, and arXiv:1702.08430 to establish definitions and comparison baselines.

Extract the equations or quoted scalings for radiative-decay lifetime and X-ray flux, relic fraction, average momentum or equivalent thermal-WDM mass, free-streaming or half-mode scale, and BBN decay effects.

Construct a comparison matrix—not a claimed new numerical scan—listing representative mass and mixing bands that pass BBN alone, then mark whether each band is removed or retained after X-ray, abundance, and structure constraints.
For non-resonant production, verify whether the mixing needed for the relic density conflicts with X-ray or Lyman-alpha bounds; record the mass range and assumptions behind each conclusion.

For resonant Shi–Fuller production, record the required lepton-asymmetry range or resonance history when stated, and determine how the allowed mixing changes when the sterile state is all of the dark matter versus a warm subcomponent.

For mixed cold-plus-warm models, extract the allowed warm fraction and the corresponding suppression scale, checking whether BBN changes materially or merely remains automatically satisfied for sufficiently long-lived keV states.

For modified-interaction and freeze-in/freeze-out scenarios, identify how production changes the mixing–abundance relation and whether the resulting parameter region survives simultaneous BBN, X-ray, and structure constraints.

Cross-check the heavy-HNL regime by mapping lifetime and decay temperature qualitatively onto BBN effects, including temporary matter domination and injection into mesons, photons, charged leptons, or neutrinos.

Use exact citations and, where needed, figure captions to distinguish published allowed regions from the team’s synthesis; report uncertainties caused by structure-formation data choices and flavor assumptions.

Conclude with a hierarchy of robust versus model-dependent viability statements and list open gaps, especially the scarcity of recent papers combining keV dark matter production with a full BBN treatment.
success_criteria: A constraint-combination table that distinguishes BBN-only allowance from joint viability after X-ray, abundance, and structure constraints.
A clear result for non-resonant production, resonant production, mixed cold-plus-warm models, and nonstandard interaction or freeze-in benchmarks.
Quantitative or semi-quantitative mass, mixing, warm-fraction, and lepton-asymmetry information wherever published sources provide it.
A separate treatment of keV dark matter and MeV–GeV HNLs, avoiding the incorrect application of late-decay BBN bounds to sufficiently long-lived keV dark matter.
Every externally sourced conclusion supported by an arXiv citation, with uncertainty and dependence on production and structure-formation assumptions stated explicitly.

issues.text: The direction risks conflating the 2024 BBN analysis of MeV–GeV heavy neutral leptons with keV sterile-neutrino dark matter. It must explicitly classify each paper by mass regime, lifetime, abundance, and production mechanism before combining results.

The requested quantitative surviving regions may not be recoverable from published plots or captions with the available tools. Do not report interpolated numerical boundaries as published results; label plot-read values as approximate and preserve the source assumptions.

The search plan needs an auditable coverage record: exact queries, arXiv date cutoff, inclusion and exclusion criteria, and checks for versions or papers whose titles do not mention BBN. This is important if the conclusion is that no 2025–2026 keV-DM-plus-BBN paper exists.

The 19-call budget is not operationalized. The plan should prioritize a small set of primary papers and reserve calls for full-text verification and citation extraction rather than attempting exhaustive downloads, figure extraction, and duplicate searches.

A comparison matrix cannot generally establish joint viability by marking independent constraints as passed or failed. X-ray, relic-density, lepton-asymmetry, momentum-distribution, and structure limits can share correlated production assumptions. The synthesis must distinguish published combined scans from an approximation assembled by the team.

The direction should not imply a universal mass–mixing band for resonant, freeze-in, freeze-out, or self-interaction scenarios. These mechanisms can decouple abundance from mixing, so results should be reported as conditional benchmark points or regions with all extra parameters stated.

The treatment of BBN needs a sharper lifetime criterion for keV states versus late-decaying HNLs, including whether Delta N_eff or thermalization is relevant even when electromagnetic or hadronic decay injection is negligible.

The two directions substantially duplicate the literature search and extraction work. Assign d-01 the publication inventory and evidence ledger, and restrict d-02 to constraint-combination logic and model-dependence checks to avoid spending calls on repeated searches.

Title: BBN Constraint on Heavy Neutrino Production and Decay
Authors: Yu-Ming Chen, Yue Zhang
Year: 2024
Abstract: We explore the big-bang nucleosynthesis (BBN) constraint on heavy neutrino that is a mixture of gauge singlet fermion and active neutrinos in the Standard Model. We work in the minimal model with only two parameters, the heavy neutrino mass $m_4$ and the mixing parameter $|U_{a4}|^2$, where $a=e$, $μ$, or $τ$ stands for the active neutrino flavor. We show that both the early universe production mechanism and decay products of the heavy neutrino are determined by $m_4$ and $|U_{a4}|^2$, with little room for further assumptions. This predictivity allows us to present a portrait of the entire BBN excluded parameter space. Our analysis includes various effects including temporary matter domination, energy injections in the form of charged mesons, photons and light neutrinos. The BBN constraint is complementary to terrestrial search for heavy neutrinos (heavy neutral leptons) behind the origin of neutrino masses and portal to the dark sector.

arXiv ID: 1702.08430
Title: keV sterile neutrino Dark Matter
Authors: Alexander Merle
Year: 2017
Abstract: We give an overview of the current status of keV sterile neutrino Dark Matter. After a short introduction, we start by a general discussion of non-thermal production of Dark Matter, which applies to the three most commonly discussed mechanisms to produce sterile neutrino Dark Matter in the Universe: non-resonant, resonant, and decay production. The main goal in each case is to compute the momentum distribution function $f(p,t)$, which incorporates the full information about the Dark Matter setting under consideration, at least in what concerns its cosmological aspects. While some difficulties lie in the actual computation of this quantity, it is decisive to obtain bounds from cosmic structure formation, which turn out to be the most crucial ones to distinguish different types of production. We will introduce these bounds and we put the resulting limits into a proper context, thereby illustrating that a significant amount of relevant parameter space is available, part of which is testable in particular by Lyman-$α$ data.

An unidentified 3.55 keV X-ray line in stacked spectra of galaxies and clusters raises the interesting
possibility that it originates from the decay of sterile neutrino dark matter. In this work, we
explore mixed sterile neutrino dark matter models that combine cold dark matter and warmer
sterile neutrino dark matter produced through lepton number-driven active-to-sterile neutrino
transformation. We analyze the sensitivity of the sterile neutrino spectra on active-sterile mixing
and on initial neutrino lepton numbers. Furthermore, we assess the viability of these models with
estimates of the number of subhalos formed as the host sites of satellite galaxies.
I. INTRODUCTION
The nature of dark matter, which comprises nearly all
of the non-relativistic matter in the universe, remains a
mystery. An interesting piece of the dark matter puzzle
is the discovery of an unidentified 3 .55 keV X-ray line
in stacked spectra of galaxies and clusters [1, 2]. One
possible explanation for this X-ray line is the decay of
sterile neutrino dark matter with a mass of 7 .1 keV that
decays into the aforementioned X-ray photon and an
equally energetic active neutrino. While there is vigorous
debate surrounding the interpretation of this feature in
the data, it remains an intriguing possibility that these
X-ray spectra may probe particle physics beyond the
Standard Model.
Sterile neutrinos are an attractive dark matter particle
candidate [3–6]. Other than through gravitation, sterile
neutrinos do not interact with Standard Model particles
unless they mix with active neutrinos or are affected
by Beyond Standard Model (BSM) interactions. They
can be incorporated into a minimal extension of the
Standard Model to account for non-zero neutrino masses
[7, 8]. There are a variety of proposed mechanisms
to create the observed density of sterile neutrino dark
matter through active-to-sterile neutrino scattering-
induced transformation [9–11] and other mechanisms
with BSM interactions [12–17].
What does it mean if the X-ray line is the result
of the decay of virialized sterile neutrino dark matter?
The sterile neutrino mass is well determined as twice
the X-ray line energy. The decay would imply active-
sterile mixing, characterized by a vacuum mixing angle,
sin2 2θ. Measurements of this mixing angle – e.g., as in
Refs. [1, 2] – need to assume that all of the dark matter
in the telescope’s field of view is sterile neutrino dark
matter. While models can be constructed to create the
observationally-inferred quantity of sterile neutrino dark
matter, their resulting distributions and the subsequent
structure formation that ensues may be at odds with
observations on small scales.

The cold dark matter paradigm may have tension with
observations on small scales [18], particularly related to
dwarf galaxy counts and dark matter density profiles.
Active-to-sterile neutrino transformation through the
Dodelson-Widrow mechanism [9] or the lepton-number
driven Shi-Fuller mechanism [10] produce warmer dark
matter distributions, which provides an attractive model
to alleviate this tension. However, these distributions
may be too warm to create the observed small scale
structure [19, 20], but this issue may be alleviated by
other BSM mechanisms that produce colder spectra [12–
17].
In this work, we consider mixed sterile neutrino dark
matter models where the term “mixed” plays a double
meaning. On one hand, the 7.1 keV sterile neutrino
quantum mechanically mixes with each of the three
active neutrinos allowing for three distinct channels to
resonantly produce sterile neutrino dark matter through
the Shi-Fuller mechanism. On the other hand, we
examine a statistical mixture of these warmer sterile
neutrinos and cold dark matter to comprise the full
observed dark matter content [12, 21, 22]. While there
are multiple avenues to constrain these dark matter
models with small scale structure [23], we focus on the
formation of dark matter subhalos that could be the site
of Milky Way satellites, as in Refs. [19, 20]. The goal
of this work is to explore the phase space of possibilities
of mixed sterile neutrino dark matter spectra produced
by this model and to discuss constraints on these models
through the lens of small scale structure formation.
We are agnostic on the identity of the cold dark matter
particle in these mixed sterile neutrino dark matter
models, as long as their distribution can be treated as
that of cold dark matter. The Shi-Fuller mechanism
requires an initial neutrino lepton number that is many
orders of magnitude larger than the baryon-to-photon
ratio, yet small compared to any detectable limits
from observations of the Cosmic Microwave Background
(CMB) or Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN) yields.
There are many proposed mechanisms to create such a
lepton number [24–28], and we are agnostic to which
mechanism, so long as the asymmetries are created at
T >∼ GeV.

INTRODUCTION
The nature of dark matter (DM), after many decades of
investigation, still lies beyond our knowledge. A number
of candidates belonging to the class of weakly interact-
ing massive particles (WIMPs) [1] have received a lot of
attention from the theoretical and experimental point of
view. However, so far, none of the attempts to capture
incontestable evidence of the existence of WIMP DM has
given positive results. This situation makes other species
of DM candidates more and more appealing [2]. Among
those, sterile neutrinos with a mass of the order of a few
keV proved to have all the credentials to play the role of
dark matter [3–5], in addition to the fact that their ex-
istence could be motivated also by reasons of symmetry
and aesthetics of the Standard Model (SM), and by the
need of giving mass to the SM active neutrinos.
One of the main diﬀerences between sterile neutrinos
and WIMPs resides in the way in which they have been
produced in the early Universe. While WIMPs would
have been thermally produced in great abundance and
reached equilibrium with the primordial plasma before
freezing-out due to the cooling and expansion of the Uni-
verse, the most natural way for sterile neutrinos to be
produced is through neutrino oscillation and collisions in
theprimordialplasma, asdescribedﬁrstbyDodelsonand
Widrow (DW) [6]. In this scenario, one or more active
neutrino states can mix with a sterile stateνs, which is
our DM candidate. During the propagation, neutrinos
scatter with particles in the plasma through weak inter-
actions, and this causes the mixed state to collapse to
a weak interaction eigenstate (active neutrino), thereby
giving origin to a non-negligible abundance of frozen-in
sterile neutrinos.
In the DW mechanism, the parameters that deter-
mine the ﬁnal abundance of the sterile neutrino DM
are the mass of the sterile neutrino ms and its mix-
ing with the active species θ. The case in which the
entire content of dark matter is constituted by sterile
neutrinos is represented by a straight line in this pa-
rameter space. More complicated mechanisms of pro-
duction, such as the Shi-Fuller mechanism [7] which de-
scribes resonant production, or non-standard cosmologi-
cal or particle physics scenarios in which the production
occurs [8–16], depend on more parameters and modify
the region of the parameter space where the condition
Ωsh2 = Ω DMh2 = 0.12 [17] is satisﬁed. In the stan-
dard DW scenario, the values ofms and sin2(2θ) that
correspond to Ωsh2 = Ω DMh2 = 0.12, are ruled out
by constraints coming from X-ray observations [18, 19].
However, non-standard self-interactions (NSSI) can as-
sist in eﬃcient production of sterile neutrinos in such a
way that the parameter space region originating the cor-
rect abundance of sterile neutrinos is enlarged and the
X-ray constraints evaded, which has been demonstrated
for Dirac neutrinos in Refs. [20–22].

independent framework. Using the formalism of eﬀec-
tive ﬁeld theory (EFT) to incorporate neutrino NSSI,
we study the production of sterile neutrino dark mat-
ter through the Dodelson-Widrow mechanism. We study
here generic ﬂavor-diagonal NSSI for Majorana neutri-
nos; they can be mediated by a scalar, pseudoscalar or
an axial-vector particle. Focusing only on one type of
NSSI at a time, we discover that the interplay between
the NSSI contribution to the interaction rate and the

well as larger mixing angles. We have not limited our

such a “cocktail DM”, where sterile neutrinos forms only

Abstract
A sterile neutrino with a keV-scale mass is a compelling dark matter candidate. We propose a new
production mechanism involving the decay and annihilation of a complex scalar singlet with a Higgs
portal coupling which develops a vacuum expectation value. The interactions of the resulting pseudo
Nambu-Goldstone boson may thermalise the dark sector. We determine the region of parameter space

freeze-out.

I. INTRODUCTION
Although the Standard Model (SM) is a very successful model of nature, it remains in-
complete. Notably, both the nature of dark matter (DM), which accounts for one quarter of
the energy density of the Universe [1], and the origin of neutrino masses are unknown. The
simplest explanation of the former is in terms of a new particle which is stable on cosmolog-
ical timescales, interacts at most weakly with known baryonic matter, and is cold. Neutrinos
themselves were one of the early dark matter candidates, but have long since been ruled out
because their contribution to the Universe’s energy density is much too small and their light-
ness contradicts our understanding of large scale structure formation. An intriguing possibility
for dark matter, however, is that it is comprised of sterile neutrinos with keV-scale mass [2],
thereby linking DM to the neutrino mass problem.
Right-handed sterile neutrinos are a natural extension of the SM from a theoretical point
of view, as they serve as the missing right-handed partners of the left-handed active neutrinos,
moreover they can explain tiny neutrino masses through the seesaw mechanism [3–6]. Three
right-handed neutrinos are suﬃcient for simultaneously describing dark matter, via a single
keV-scale sterile neutrino, and generating neutrino masses, via two heavy sterile neutrinos [7].
Sterile neutrinos with a keV-scale mass are generally warm dark matter candidates (WDM)
which suppress power at small scales and therefore may play some role in resolving small scale
structure issues, although explanations involving baryonic physics or self-interacting DM have
been more favoured recently [8]. Sterile neutrino DM with 7.1 keV mass has also been suggested
as a possible explanation of the 3.55 keV x-ray line [9, 10]. More generally, the keV scale is an
intriguing frontier to consider because both the Tremaine-Gunn bound [11] and Lyman-α data
[12] forbid fermionic DM from being lighter thanO(keV).
SuchlightDMcannotbefrozenoutbyelectroweakinteractions, becauseinthatcaseitwould
be overabundant [13]. A simple, viable production mechanism for keV-scale DM is freeze-in [14,
15], where its abundance is initially negligible and is slowly produced via decay, annihilation or
mixing controlled by a small coupling. In the presence of active-sterile neutrino mixing, sterile
neutrinos are most straightforwardly produced via neutrino oscillations [2, 16, 17]. However,
non-resonant neutrino oscillations has already been ruled out as the source of the overall DM
abundance due to a combination of x-ray and Ly-α constraints [18]. Even in presence of a
large lepton asymmetry, resonant neutrino oscillations [19] are still strongly restricted by Ly-α
data [12].
A minimal extension of this scenario involves the production of sterile neutrinos from scalar
3

--- Page 4 ---
boson decay [20–31]. Within this, we will consider the possibility that the scalar is itself frozen-
in [25, 27–29, 31], thus production is a two-step process. Initially, the scalar boson is produced;
subsequently, it decays to sterile neutrinos. Existing studies have focused only on a real scalar
ﬁeld which is odd under aZ2 symmetry. After spontaneous symmetry breaking of the discrete
symmetry, the scalar boson develops a vacuum expectation value and generates the sterile
neutrino mass. Thus, the coupling controlling the scalar decay to sterile neutrinos is directly
proportional to the sterile neutrino mass. The interactions of the sterile neutrinos (and often
of the frozen-in scalar) are feeble enough that they do not thermalise. However, the breaking
of the global discreteZ2 symmetry can lead to the formation of domain walls [32], which is an
intrinsic problem of this real scalar singlet model.
In this work we propose an elegant way to avoid domain walls by promoting the discreteZ2
symmetry to a globalU(1) symmetry, and study its phenomenological implications. It requires
the introduction of a complex scalar ﬁeld, rather than a real scalar, to generate a sterile neutrino
mass term after spontaneous symmetry breaking. This small change drastically modiﬁes the
phenomenology of sterile neutrino production in the early Universe. Interactions involving the
pseudo Nambu-Goldstone boson (pNGB) can enable the frozen-in scalar sector to reach both
chemical and kinetic equilibrium and thus to thermalise with a temperatureTφ <T (the model
is therefore a concrete example of thermal DM withTφ ⁄= T, which was recently classiﬁed
in [33]). It may even bring the sterile neutrinos into kinetic (and chemical) equilibrium. Since
the interactions eventually go out of equilibrium and the sterile neutrino comoving number
density becomes ﬁxed at some temperature below the heavy scalar mass, it can be said to
freeze-in and freeze-out.
This scenario is a departure from the usual case, as generally neither kinetic nor chemical
equilibrium is reached for frozen-in ﬁelds which explain the observed dark matter abundance. In
this work, we also include quantum statistical factors and apply the full relativistic treatment,
making approximations where applicable. This is important in the context of the light sterile
neutrino and pNGB.
The paper is organised as follows. In Sec. II we outline the production mechanism in general
terms and introduce the model. Sterile neutrino production is discussed in Sec. III, and the
temperature of the dark sector is computed in Sec. IV. The thermalisation of the scalar sector
is addressed in Sec. V, and the thermalisation of the sterile neutrinos in Sec. VI. Finally, we
discuss the results and conclude in Sec. VII. In the appendices we present some technical details
related to scattering in the scalar sector.

II. THE MODEL
The freeze-in mechanism [14, 15] is now a well-known scenario for the production of particles
whose initial abundance is assumed to be negligible, possibly due to the inﬂationary dynamics.1
A key feature of this mechanism is that interactions between the frozen-in particles and the
thermal bath of SM particles (which has temperatureT) is suﬃciently feeble that the former
never equilibrate with the latter. This feeble interaction is due to a very small coupling between
the two sectors, which can nevertheless be technically natural [35]. The production predomi-
nantly takes place at temperatures of the order of the masses of the parent particles, as long
as the interactions are renormalisable.
The mechanism we consider in this paper is schematically illustrated in Fig. 1. It involves a
second iteration of the freeze-in scenario.2 A complex scalarφ (which consists of a heavy scalar
ϕ and pNGBα, see Eqn. (3)) and sterile neutrinoN both have negligible initial abundance.

In this article, we take minimality as the guiding principle and explore simplified models where
the mixing of sterile neutrino with the Standard Model active neutrino is the only portal for it to
interact with other known particles. Under this assumption, there is little ambiguity about the fate of

The interplay between the heavy neutrino lifetime and its thermal contact with the Standard
Model plasma is a useful guideline for our study. Note that only sufficiently weakly-coupled heavy
neutrino with a small mixing parameter can have a lifetime comparable to the BBN time scale. For
sufficiently small mixing, the heavy neutrino may not establish thermal equilibrium with the Standard
Model particles. To set the most conservative limit, we assume it begins with zero initial population
after inflation and any abundance must be built up through the mixing with active neutrinos. The
BBN constraint on heavy neutrino can be evaded if the mixing parameter is tiny so that the heavy
neutrino is rarely produced, or if the mixing is so large that the heavy neutrino decays away well
before the onset of BBN. As a result, the BBN constraint only applies to a window of intermediate
mixing values. The goal of this work is to quantify the position of this window as a function of the
heavy neutrino mass.

We conclude with some caveats to these results which
lead us to future work. In this work, we focused on
the properties of our three-to-one mixed sterile neutrino
dark matter model, where the lepton number-driven
transformation of all three active neutrino species into
sterile neutrinos is complemented by cold dark matter.
In particular, we explored the properties of the spectra
produced in these models and their connection with
astrophysical constraints.
In our exploration, we used the scattering rates from
Ref. [11] instead of those used in more sophisticated
calculations, for example as in Ref. [50]. While
updated scattering rates will change the specifics of the
conclusions, the overall properties and discussion of these
mixed sterile neutrino dark matter models will remain
unchanged. For example, with the higher scattering rate
in Ref. [50], we expect the boundary curve in Fig. 12 to
have a similar shape, but the maximum sin 2 2θastro will
be lower and the maximum fraction of sterile neutrino
dark matter will be lower as well. This is because the
higher scattering rate will boost non-resonant production

--- Page 9 ---

and suppress resonant production.
Another question involves mixing between the three
active neutrinos. In principle, a 4 × 4-mixing matrix
would describe the neutrino sector of these mixed
sterile neutrino dark matter models [51]. However,
because the mixing angles considered are so small,
there is negligible loss in independently approaching
transformation in each active-sterile channel. The
3× 3 mixing between the active neutrinos (and the
anti-neutrinos) may present non-trivial quantum kinetic
evolution, especially when the lepton numbers in the
three flavors are different [52, 53]. While it is
possible that resonances can efficiently redistribute and
equilibrate the lepton numbers amongst the three flavors,
the high scattering rates at T∼ 300 MeV may suppress
this process. Nevertheless, if we look at Fig. 6, we
see that in the three-to-one model with equal mixing
angles and lepton numbers, the three lepton numbers
have similar evolutions, so we feel that this may have
little effect on these models. However, if we investigate
mixing schema with different mixing angles for the three
channels, this may cause the lepton number evolution
of the different flavors to diverge, and this effect may
become more pronounced.
Structure formation is a valuable approach to constrain
dark matter production models. In this work we
used an approach to estimate the number of subhalos
produced and constrain these models in connection
with the number of observed Milky Way satellites (see,
e.g., Refs. [19, 20]). This approach doesn’t appear to
be grossly out of line with other structure-formation
based approaches to constraining dark matter spectra
[23, 35]. While we do not expect any drastic changes
to the conclusions drawn in this work, other structure
formation-based approaches should be incorporated
when discussing models at the edge of viability as
discussed in Fig. 12.

1. Introduction
If there is one thing the astro- and/or particle physics communities agree on, it is that one of
the major questions of contemporary science is about the true nature of Dark Matter (DM). This
substance makes up more than 80% of the full matter content of the Universe, but up to now we
have not yet ﬁgured out what is behind. While we are somewhat certain of several aspects of DM
(its energy density, its rough distribution today, and the fact that it was crucial for cosmic structure
formation), there are other things we do not know precisely (its identity, its production mechanism,
its momentum distribution after production). While there are strong hints towards DM being made
out of new elementary particles, our partial lack of knowledge suggests that we should question old
believes and possibly re-evaluate certain statements made in the literature.
In the literature, the “standard” candidate for DM is regarded to be a Weakly Interacting Mas-
sive Particle (WIMP). However, while WIMPs do have a lot of theory motivation behind them, we
cannot ignore the fact that we have not yet seen an unambiguous signal. On the contrary, on-going
experiments push our limits further and further, such that, given the lack of a detection, we must
start to seriously consider alternative possibilities.
Taking a step back, we should ask which non-WIMP particle ticks all the boxes for DM. One
natural candidate is a sterile neutrino N . This particle with mass mN is electrically neutral and
interacts even more feebly than an “active” neutrino να (with ﬂavours α = e, µ, τ), namely by
vertices suppressed by the small active-sterile mixing angle θα. Given that sterile neutrinos can be
rather massive, they would certainly be able to act as DM, provided that they are produced in the
early Universe in the right amount and with a suitable momentum spectrum [1].
Before we start, let us remark that the most complete source of information and references in
existence at the moment is the White Paper on keV sterile neutrino Dark Matter [2].

would be warm. The origin of this statement is in parts historic, but when looking at the details it is
often just not the case. Formally, a thermal distribution would amount to the following momentum

The most natural approach is to produce sterile neutrinos by their admixture to the active-
neutrino sector [ 4, 5, 6, 7], which exploits the fact that any reaction producing active neutrinos

mixing angles are non-zero. This could gradually produce enough sterile neutrinos to explain the
observed amount of DM, but the resulting spectrum would feature too many particles with rather
large momenta, making this setting similar to a hot DM case and thus excluded by data.

early Universe, a suitable value of which can resonantly enhance the transitions from active to
sterile neutrinos [6, 8, 9, 10]. While the origin of such an asymmetry has to be explained at ﬁrst,

many sterile neutrinos at a very speciﬁc combination of momentum and temperature. Thus, in the

comprising a non-thermal distribution. If this peak is located at a comparatively small momentum,
i.e., a big fraction of the sterile neutrinos are not very fast, the resulting spectrum should be “cooler”

150–450 MeV sterile neutrinos and finds severe constraints from helium-4 and
deuterium. A large active-neutrino lepton asymmetry can relax those bounds;
the consistent scenario has Delta N_eff approximately 3.2–3.4.

6. Nashwan Sabti, Andrii Magalich, and Anastasiia Filimonova,
   “An Extended Analysis of Heavy Neutral Leptons during Big Bang
   Nucleosynthesis,” arXiv:2006.07387v3 (2020).

sensitivity to lifetimes as short as 0.03–0.05 s depending on the mixing

  large flavor asymmetry. Its abstract supports a viable span of roughly

  mass-mixing contour.

- X-ray constraints:
  The searched 2026 resonant-production abstract explicitly identifies
  next-generation X-ray telescopes as necessary to test the remaining
  parameter space. The COSI forecast paper, arXiv:2610.17217v1, covers
  decaying-DM masses from 0.4 to 10 MeV and projects more than an order of
  magnitude improvement in lifetime sensitivity, but it is a forecast and
  not a complete sterile-neutrino exclusion analysis.

- Lyman-alpha constraints:
  None of the returned abstracts provides a quantitative Lyman-alpha
  lower bound on the sterile-neutrino mass. Therefore no defensible
  Lyman-alpha mass threshold is reported here.

- MeV–GeV HNL/BBN constraints:

Abstract: Bursty or (rotation-induced) pulsed coherent radio emission from pulsars, magnetars, and fast radio transients originates in some of the most extreme environments in the Universe. However, the exact physical mechanism behind the scenes remains poorly understood. ALMA2040 will allow for systematic exploration of the millimeter-wavelength spectral window for pulsars and fast radio transients for the very first time, offering unprecedented opportunities to discover new observational phenomena and advance our understanding of emission physics. Abstract: One of the most striking aspects of a flat band is not merely its lack of dispersion, but that it reduces the single-particle kinetic energy to a very small scale, allowing interaction effects to become the dominant energy scale in the low-energy physics. This picture has underpinned concepts such as flat-band ferromagnetism, flat-band superconductivity, and localized magnons. A more fundamental question, however, remains. Flat bands belong to the language of single-particle or linear-spin-wave physics; whether they survive as protected sharp excitations in a genuine many-body quantum magnet, or merely provide a skeleton of spectral weight left by the noninteracting picture, remains unclear. We study the spin-1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the edge-centered honeycomb lattice to examine this question. In contrast to flat bands in geometrically frustrated magnets such as kagome, this lattice has a 2:3 sublattice imbalance that renders the intersublattice coupling matrix rectangular, whose null space gives rise to a flat band at the single-particle level. The same imbalance stabilizes a ferrimagnetic ground state through the Lieb--Mattis theorem and leads to an edge-site-localized flat magnon in linear spin-wave theory. Combining linear spin-wave theory, sign-problem-free stochastic series expansion quantum Monte Carlo, and stochastic analytic continuation, we find that quantum fluctuations transform this harmonic flat mode into a broad continuum whose centroid is about 1.55J and nearly dispersionless along the high-symmetry path. Sublattice imbalance thus offers an unfrustrated route that unifies flat bands and ferrimagnetism, and suggests that flat-band geometry organizes many-body spectral weight rather than giving rise to a protected quasiparticle.

Abstract: While graphene/n-type silicon (Gr/n-Si) and PEDOT:PSS/n-Si solar cells offer a cost-effective alternative to conventional photovoltaics, achieving simultaneous high power conversion efficiency (PCE) and long-term environmental stability remains a formidable challenge. Here, we report the synergistic enhancement of both performance and stability in a planar trilayer PEDOT:PSS/Gr/n-Si Schottky junction architecture. By systematically benchmarking this hybrid device against pristine Gr/n-Si and PEDOT:PSS/n-Si reference cells fabricated on untextured substrates, we isolate the fundamental optoelectronic and barrier functions of the carbon lattice. Comprehensive analyses reveal that the PEDOT:PSS layer simultaneously functions as an anti-reflection coating, a moderate p-type dopant for the underlying graphene, and a conductivity enhancer, collectively optimizing interfacial charge transport. Consequently, the trilayer device achieves a PCE of 8.52%, markedly outperforming the pristine Gr/n-Si reference cell (4.56%). Crucially, the atomic impermeability of the graphene sheet serves as a robust environmental barrier. While bare PEDOT:PSS/n-Si junctions retained only ~29% of their initial efficiency after 75 days of ambient exposure, graphene shields the active junction from moisture-induced degradation of the hygroscopic PEDOT:PSS overlayer. This enables the trilayer device to retain approximately 90% of its initial efficiency over the same 75-day period. The complementary roles of graphene as both a highly crystalline charge transport interface and an impermeable protective barrier establish a highly effective strategy for engineering high-efficiency, environmentally stable hybrid photovoltaics.

Abstract: A confident detection of orbital eccentricity in gravitational-wave signals from black hole-neutron star systems would be a strong indicator of their dynamical formation origin. While eccentric waveform models have recently been developed, their validity for analyzing black hole--neutron star signals has yet to be tested against numerical-relativity simulations. Building upon our previous study of quasicircular black hole--neutron star mergers, we perform simulations of a subset of these systems with orbital eccentricities around five times larger than those inferred for GW200105_162426. Additionally, we perform simulations with magnetized matter to assess whether trapped $g$-mode oscillations persist in strongly magnetized disks. Regarding the emitted gravitational-wave signal, we find that the effective one-body waveform model SEOBNRv5EHM shows reasonable agreement unless tidal contributions become important, and the inspiral-only post-Newtonian models pyEFPE/pyEFPEHM show larger disagreement in the late inspiral. For the equal-mass system, which has the largest effective tidal deformability, eccentric tidal corrections have a small but noticeable impact on the phase, $\sim0.1$ rad. We find an almost negligible impact of eccentricity on the properties of the remnant black hole, and differences of up to a factor of two in the remnant disk mass. Trapped $g$ modes in the accretion disks have the same frequency regardless of the eccentricity, confirming that they depend mainly on the properties of the remnant black hole. We find that when accretion disks are strongly magnetized, they become less dense and have less pronounced structure, and that the trapped $g$ modes previously identified in the unmagnetized cases are efficiently damped.

Abstract: Convergent beam electron diffraction (CBED), recently demonstrated on two-dimensional (2D) materials, offers a number of interesting applications such as imaging atomic in- and out-of plane shifts, interlayer distances, and individual adsorbates. In this study, we show how CBED allows for atomic-precision imaging of individual defects in 2D materials using one single-shot intensity measurement. Abstract: Fractional spin excitations in low-dimensional and frustrated magnets are commonly associated with sporadic spin fluctuations, as observed in quantum spin liquids, spin ices, and other complex magnetic states. In this study, we investigate the spin dynamics in the amplitude-modulated magnetic ground state of AgCuVO$_4$, a spin-1/2 chain compound with competing intrachain interactions, by muon spectroscopy. Our data reveal a Gaussian decay of muon polarization that remains remarkably resilient against applied magnetic fields---a behavior often interpreted as evidence of emergent sporadic spin dynamics. However, density functional theory calculations of muon stopping sites and their quadrupolar level-crossing resonance spectra suggest an alternative mechanism: a two-state model where the muon randomly hops between two nearby sites, eventually equilibrating across both on a microsecond timescale via quantum delocalization. These findings provide a microscopic explanation for the field-resilient muon polarization and indicate that such behavior may not always stem from intrinsic spin fluctuations, but can also arise from non-equilibrium muon dynamics.

Abstract: We investigate the potential of surface detector arrays to identify ultra-high-energy neutrinos using vertical air showers with zenith angle $θ\leq 60^\circ$, a region largely unexplored in current searches. The method exploits the enhanced electromagnetic component at ground level arising from energetic leptons produced in neutrino interactions. Using detailed air-shower and detector simulations, we show that observables sensitive to the electromagnetic and muonic content provide genuine discrimination between neutrino-induced and hadron-induced showers. This is demonstrated both with idealized shower quantities and with realistic detector-level signals based on water-Cherenkov and scintillator detectors. The corresponding neutrino identification efficiency is used to derive the effective mass and, primarily, the effective area of the array under background-rejection requirements appropriate to targeted multi-messenger searches. Although not competitive with inclined-shower searches under the stringent background rejection factors required for diffuse-flux analyses, this approach establishes the feasibility of a vertical detection channel, extending the field of view of surface arrays and providing a complementary tool for multi-messenger observations of transient sources.

Abstract: Embodied AI agents in Augmented Reality (AR) could enable more natural collaboration in immersive analytics by engaging users through spatial, conversational, and visual interaction. However, designing such agents requires careful attention to context. We propose a preliminary conceptual framework for context-aware design of embodied agents structured around three dimensions of spatial, social, and semantic. This framework is further categorised into embeddedness (how agents are situated in the contexts) and awareness (how agents perceive and respond to the contexts). Abstract: Quantum measurements not only extract information but also reshape quantum evolution through measurement backaction. Here, we investigate periodic conditional measurements, in which coherent evolution is repeatedly interrupted by local measurements. Abstract: Assembling defect-free arrays of neutral atoms requires real-time rearrangement of stochastically loaded optical tweezers. Conventional rearrangement methods shuttle atoms sequentially, whereas high-speed spatial light modulators (SLMs) can move all atoms in parallel, which scales more favorably as the array size grows. For fast parallel rearrangement, the sequence of holograms displayed on the SLM should be computed more rapidly than the SLM refresh rate, and there should be phase continuity between successive holograms to minimize transient intensity fluctuations. We calculate holograms analytically by adding together the complex fields needed to produce each individual trap, and we ramp the phase of each trap linearly as it moves to its target location. Trap positions enter as continuous variables, rather than tied to points on a grid, so the method provides high positioning accuracy. Using a single GPU, we compute each intermediate hologram in 0.284 ms, considerably faster than the SLM refresh time of 0.696 ms, so the rearrangement speed is hardware-limited. In each step, we use the free processing time to iteratively optimize the holograms for equal intensity across the traps, decreasing trap non-uniformity to 1.24% during rearrangement at no cost in total time. Starting from an array of 256 sites loaded stochastically with $^{87}$Rb atoms, we assemble a 100-atom array in under 20 ms with a rearrangement survival probability of 99.31(12)% per atom. This rearrangement increases the temperature of the atoms by 9(3) $μ$K, which is small compared to the trap depth of 480 $μ$K. Our method can also move individual atoms axially, enabling transport in different planes. We demonstrate this capability with a rearrangement protocol where one set of atoms leapfrogs over another.

arXiv ID: 2410.07343
Title: BBN Constraint on Heavy Neutrino Production and Decay
Authors: Yu-Ming Chen, Yue Zhang
Year: 2024
Abstract: We explore the big-bang nucleosynthesis (BBN) constraint on heavy neutrino that is a mixture of gauge singlet fermion and active neutrinos in the Standard Model. We work in the minimal model with only two parameters, the heavy neutrino mass $m_4$ and the mixing parameter $|U_{a4}|^2$, where $a=e$, $μ$, or $τ$ stands for the active neutrino flavor. We show that both the early universe production mechanism and decay products of the heavy neutrino are determined by $m_4$ and $|U_{a4}|^2$, with little room for further assumptions. This predictivity allows us to present a portrait of the entire BBN excluded parameter space. Our analysis includes various effects including temporary matter domination, energy injections in the form of charged mesons, photons and light neutrinos. The BBN constraint is complementary to terrestrial search for heavy neutrinos (heavy neutral leptons) behind the origin of neutrino masses and portal to the dark sector.

Our analysis includes various effects including temporary matter domination, energy injections in the form of charged mesons, photons and light neutrinos. The BBN constraint is complementary to terrestrial search for heavy neutrinos (heavy neutral leptons) behind the origin of neutrino masses and portal to the dark sector.

Title: No Hiding in the Dark: Cosmological Bounds on Heavy Neutral Leptons with Dark Decay Channels
Authors: P. S. Bhupal Dev, Quan-feng Wu, Xun-Jie Xu
Year: 2025
Abstract: Heavy neutral leptons (HNLs) are well-motivated new physics candidates. The mixing of sub-GeV HNLs with active neutrinos is severely constrained by cosmology. In particular, the success of Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN) requires the HNL lifetime to be shorter than about 0.02 sec if they were in thermal equilibrium, thus excluding a wide range of mixing angles accessible to terrestrial experiments. In order to justify the laboratory searches in this cosmologically-forbidden region, it is often argued that adding new dark sector decay modes of HNLs can evade the stringent BBN constraint. Our result has major implications for laboratory searches of HNLs.

arXiv ID: 2410.06970
Title: Relaxing Limits from Big Bang Nucleosynthesis on Heavy Neutral Leptons with Axion-like Particles
Authors: Frank F. Deppisch, Tomás E. Gonzalo, Chayan Majumdar, Zhong Zhang
Year: 2024
Abstract: Heavy neutral leptons (HNLs) are constrained by requirements of Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN) as their decays significantly impact the formation of the primordial elements. We propose here a model where the primary decay channel for the HNLs is to an axion-like particle (ALP) and a neutrino. Consequently, HNLs can decay earlier and evade the BBN bound for lower masses, provided the ALPs themselves decay considerably later. Further cosmological and astrophysical constraints limit severely the range of validity of the ALP properties. call.result:
arXiv ID: 2510.01907
Title: Resonant production of sterile neutrino dark matter with a refined numerical scheme
Authors: Kentaro Kasai, Masahiro Kawasaki, Kai Murai
Year: 2025
Abstract: The existence of a large primordial neutrino asymmetry is an intriguing possibility, both observationally and theoretically. Such an asymmetry can lead to the resonant production of $\mathrm{keV}$-scale sterile neutrinos, which are a fascinating candidate for dark matter. In this paper, we comprehensively revisit the resonant production processes with a refined numerical analysis, adopting a dynamical discretization of momentum modes to take care of the sharpness of the resonance. We find parameter regions consistent with X-ray and Lyman-$α$ constraints for lepton-to-entropy ratio $\gtrsim \mathcal{O}(10^{-3})$ and $m_{ν_s}\gtrsim 20\,$keV. We also explore the Affleck-Dine mechanism as a possible origin for such asymmetries. While previous studies considered resonant production after lepton number generation, we numerically investigate cases where a fraction of sterile neutrinos is produced during lepton number injection. In this regime, some parameter sets can shorten the free-streaming length and reduce the required mixing angle to match the observed dark matter abundance, thereby mitigating the observational constraints.

Title: Affleck-Dine leptogenesis scenario for resonant production of sterile neutrino dark matter
Authors: Kentaro Kasai, Masahiro Kawasaki, Kai Murai
Year: 2024
Abstract: Sterile neutrino is a fascinating candidate for dark matter. In this paper, we examine the Affleck-Dine (AD) leptogenesis scenario generating a large lepton asymmetry, which can induce the resonant production of sterile neutrino dark matter via the Shi-Fuller (SF) mechanism. Finally, we discuss an enhancement of second-order gravitational waves at the L-ball decay and investigate the testability of our scenario with future gravitational wave observations.
